vignette:
Reverend Amara sits in the armchair across from me, her Bible open on her lap, a small notebook beside her. She is eighty years old, her silver hair wrapped neatly in a purple scarf that matches her Sunday dress. She speaks with a measured, deliberate calm that I have come to recognize as a carefully constructed fortress.

She came to this country forty-seven years ago, but she does not begin there. She begins with the mango tree in her father’s compound in rural Liberia. She was a girl of nine, she tells me, when the first soldiers came through the village. The mango tree was where she would hide, high among the leaves, her hands sticky with sap, her heart a trapped bird. She remembers the sound of boots on red dirt, the crack of gunfire that was always too close, the smell of smoke from houses that were not hers yet could have been.

She fled with her mother and two younger brothers. Her father stayed behind to protect the church. She never saw him again. There were weeks of walking, then months in a refugee camp in Sierra Leone. She describes the hunger—not as a memory but as a living thing that still sits in her stomach. She remembers the way her mother would give all the food to the boys, and how Amara learned not to complain. She learned to pray louder than her fear.

When she finally arrived in the United States, she was thirty-three, married to a man she had met in the camp, a quiet tailor who sewed hope into the seams of donated clothes. They settled in a small city, and she began pastoring a tiny congregation of fellow refugees in a rented storefront. She built a church from the ground up—prayer meetings, funerals, weddings, baptisms. She became known as Mama Amara, the one who could hold a broken person and not let go.

But the mango tree never left her. She tells me that at night, she still climbs it. The nightmares come without warning: the sound of boots, the crack of gunfire, the smell of smoke. She wakes gasping, her husband’s hand on her arm, her own voice already silenced by years of habit. She has not spoken of these things to anyone in her congregation. How could she? They come to her for strength, for scripture, for the promise that God makes all things new. She cannot tell them that sometimes, when the offering plate passes, she sees the face of a soldier who looked at her mother with dead eyes.

Her PCL-5 score of 42 reflects the weight she carries. She avoids certain smells—grilled meat, because it reminds her of the fires. She avoids news reports of conflict, even in distant countries. She has stopped attending church potlucks because the crowded room tightens her chest. She preaches on Sundays with the same power as always, but afterward she retreats to her office and sits in silence, her hands shaking until the tremor passes. She tells me she feels like a hypocrite. She preaches about peace but cannot find it in her own chest.

Her husband knows. He held her through the first nightmare forty years ago, and he holds her now. They have learned to move around each other in the dark. He does not ask. She does not tell. But she came to me because last month, during a funeral for a young man from her church, the wailing of his mother sent her back to that mango tree. She could not breathe. She had to excuse herself. She stood in the church bathroom and saw her own mother’s face.

She says she is tired. Not tired of living, but tired of climbing. She wants to come down from the tree. She wants to feel the ground beneath her feet and know it is safe. She turns the pages of her Bible slowly, searching for a verse that matches the ache. She says she has not found it yet, but she is still looking. That is why she is here, in this room, with me. She is still looking.
